value.overview: The Cocos Booby (Sula brewsteri) is a large tropical seabird of the eastern Pacific Ocean. It was formerly treated as a geographic form of the Brown Booby but is now recognized as a separate species by several taxonomic authorities. It breeds colonially on oceanic and coastal islands, including islands associated with Costa Rica, and spends much of its time over offshore waters. Its name refers to the important population on Cocos Island, Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Cocos Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae and the genus Sula. It includes geographically distinct populations in the eastern Pacific, including the nominate form in the Gulf of California and western Mexico and the Central and South American form Sula brewsteri etesiaca.
value.identification: This is a large, long-winged seabird with dark brown upperparts, white underparts, a dark head and neck, and a relatively slender, pointed bill. Adult males often show frosty white on the forehead, crown, or neck, while females and immature birds may have darker heads. The bill is typically yellow-based with pinkish tones toward the tip. Compared with Brown Boobies of other regions, Cocos Boobies often show more dark markings across the underwing coverts and a slimmer bill. Identification can be difficult, especially for females and young birds.
value.rangeHabitat: The Cocos Booby occurs across the tropical and subtropical eastern Pacific, from the Gulf of California and islands off western Mexico south through Central America to Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a breeding and marine species associated especially with Cocos Island and other Pacific offshore islands or waters. Birds may also be seen along the Pacific coast and over the Gulf of Nicoya, although many individuals remain offshore. It nests on rocky or vegetated islands and forages over pelagic and nearshore ocean waters.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident near breeding colonies but disperses widely over the eastern Pacific. In Costa Rica, birds occur year-round around breeding islands such as Cocos Island and in surrounding offshore waters; additional individuals may range along the Pacific coast and Gulf of Nicoya. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although nonbreeding and immature birds can travel far from colonies.
value.breeding: Cocos Boobies breed colonially on predator-free islands, rocky islets, and coastal islands. The nest is a simple platform made from sticks, vegetation, and other available material, usually placed on the ground or in low vegetation. Both parents share incubation and chick care. Breeding timing varies among colonies, and published information for Costa Rican colonies is limited. Cocos Island and other Costa Rican Pacific islands provide important nesting habitat, while nearby ocean waters supply food for adults and young.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small to medium marine fish, including flying fish and other schooling species, with squid and other marine prey also taken. Cocos Boobies usually hunt by plunge-diving from flight, entering the water at speed and pursuing prey near the surface or at moderate depth. They may forage singly or in loose groups and can associate with other seabirds where fish are concentrated.
value.behavior: Cocos Boobies are powerful fliers that spend much of the day traveling between colonies, roosts, and feeding areas. They rest on rocks, cliffs, or vegetation and show strong attachment to established breeding colonies. During the breeding season, adults defend small areas around nests and use displays, calls, and bill movements in courtship and territorial interactions. Young birds and nonbreeding individuals may wander widely across the Pacific before returning to breeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered relatively large and not currently believed to be declining at a rate that would qualify the species for a threatened category. Local colonies may nevertheless fluctuate with food availability, weather, disturbance, and breeding success.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include disturbance at breeding colonies, introduced predators on islands, entanglement or accidental capture in fishing gear, plastic pollution, and reductions in marine prey caused by overfishing or changing ocean conditions. These pressures may be particularly important for small or isolated colonies in Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect Costa Rica’s Pacific islands and surrounding marine feeding areas, prevent the introduction of rats and other predators to nesting islands, and keep people and boats away from active colonies. Responsible fishing practices, reduction of plastic waste, and long-term monitoring of Cocos Booby colonies and offshore abundance can help identify and reduce emerging threats.
